extracted.intended_audience: students learning how to write mathematical proofs (competition contestants and coursework students)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for producing informal natural-language mathematical proofs that are convincing to human readers and, in principle, compilable into formal machine-verifiable proofs. Emphasizes appropriate level-of-detail for various audiences (competition graders, mentors, peers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof definition / compilability
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical proof is an informal natural-language explanation that in principle could be compiled into a formal machine-verifiable proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goal of a proof is that it should, in principle, be translatable into a formal sequence of axioms and transformation rules (formal machine code). For practical work you do not need to perform the compilation, but your proof should be written so an expert could do it without inventing new ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convincingness (informal correctness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical proof is an informal but convincing natural-language explanation for why a statement is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convincing means the reader should be able to see how each step follows (or be able to compile them to formal steps). Avoid relying on social permission; aim for explanations that make logical dependencies clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and correctness of definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Before proving, ensure definitions are clear; many confusions stem from not having solid definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State or know the definitions you use (e.g., altitude, perpendicular, repeating decimal, infinite sum). Definitions are social conventions — once chosen, conclusions follow. If a subtle argument relies on a foundational definition, either state it or ensure your audience accepts it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate choice of primitives / stopping point
rubrics_metrics.description: You must choose which concepts to accept as 'obvious' (primitive) based on audience; you cannot define everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, in high school 2+2=4 is fine to take for granted. Choose primitives consistent with your audience; if disputable, either justify or avoid relying on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level-of-detail tailored to audience
rubrics_metrics.description: How much detail to include depends on your audience and social conventions (classroom, contest, research).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In competitions one omits routine facts; graders check whether the student could plausibly be bluffing. If a step might look like bluffing, supply more detail. For mentors/peers, include enough so they can give meaningful feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding 'bluffing' — sufficiency of demonstrated knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Include enough justification so a grader cannot reasonably think you don't actually know how to prove the omitted routine facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grader heuristic: 'is there a chance the student actually doesn't know how to prove this and is just bluffing to me?' If yes, deduct. Thus omit only truly standard steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigour equals correctness / compilability
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace the vague notion of 'rigorous' with 'correct' — the goal is that the explanation should compile to machine code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't add 'magic words' to seem rigorous; meet the compile-to-formal-proof goal. If it compiles, it's rigorous; if not, it's not a proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legality of a step: understand definitions first
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge if a step is 'legal', first check if you understand the definitions involved; lack of understanding often causes doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you can't justify a step from known definitions, you probably don't understand them (e.g., real numbers, infinite sums). Sometimes the relevant definition requires advanced coursework, in which case rely on accepted results or state assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legality of a step: try to derive it or look for counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: If you understand definitions, attempt to prove the step logically from prior statements; if you can't, there's likely a mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fast practical check is to look for counterexamples. Finding one shows the step is false. If no counterexample is found, try to derive it or isolate why you think it follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'without loss of generality' (WLOG)
rubrics_metrics.description: WLOG means the remaining cases are equivalent by symmetry; it's only legal when cases are 'obviously exactly the same'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there's any doubt a WLOG is legal, then something is wrong. Explicitly note the symmetry or provide a quick justification when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanity checks / pre-tests for whole proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no surefire shortcuts, but practical sanity checks exist: search for counterexamples, 'prove too much', and check nearby false statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these pre-tests to gain confidence quickly. For example, see if the approach would imply a similar false result (proving too much), or find unrelated counterexamples that invalidate an argument pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify key claims and modularize proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: For longer problems, isolate big claims and give self-contained proofs for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark key claims visibly and make their proofs self-contained. This helps both verification (divide-and-conquer) and exposition; small components are easier to check than the full union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize problem-specific critical steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Many competition problems have one or two crux ideas; identify them and ensure they are present and justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a grader, if a solution lacks the known crux (e.g., combining lengths/ratios in a geometry problem), it's likely wrong. Use domain knowledge to spot absent necessary ingredients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write proofs down — do not keep them in your head
rubrics_metrics.description: You should not trust a solution until it's written out; many mistakes are found only when typing or writing the solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing forces you to expose hidden gaps. Drafting also makes it easier for mentors/graders to spot errors and provide targeted feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof methods are strategies, not new rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods like induction or contradiction are strategies (patterns) within the same logical rules; learn them but don't treat them as separate logical systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand common proof patterns (analogy: openings in chess) so you can recognize and apply them when appropriate; they don't change validity requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred learning subjects for proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Graph theory and elementary number theory are especially good subjects to learn proofs with; real analysis and set theory are less suitable for beginners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose practice domains where key ideas and combinatorial reasoning appear and where definitions are accessible without heavy prerequisites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic clarity to aid human verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Cosmetic writing choices make proofs easier to read: clear definitions, paragraph breaks, isolated claims, visible structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These stylistic improvements don't fix logical errors but help mentors and graders find mistakes and understand intent. See author's separate handout for writing clarity suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checking for 'proving too much' as an error heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: When an approach seems to work, test whether it would imply additional similar results that are false; if so, the approach likely fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: suggesting a density bound would imply property P but a counterexample set with similar density lacks P — this shows the approach is invalid without further work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use counterexamples as first-line validation
rubrics_metrics.description: When in doubt about a sentence's validity in a proof, attempt to conjure a counterexample before working out formal derivations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grader practice: if a counterexample is found, you can be confident there's a mistake; this is a quick and robust check for many student errors.
